Welcome, everyone. Today is about one campaign, The Home Portrait, and we are going to walk it exactly the way a buyer lives it: the ad that stops their scroll, the ninety second quiz, the portrait we paint for them, the Design Dollars they learn about, and the lead that lands on your desk.

This is not a marketing meeting. By the end you will know what your buyer saw before they ever talked to you, and how to open that first call so it feels like a continuation, not a cold start.

Let's start with the why behind The Home Portrait. Why is it a quiz and not a contact form?

A form asks for a name, an email, and a phone number, and gives the buyer nothing back. So people give us as little as they can, and you start the first call from zero.

The quiz flips that. It asks about the home they dream of, and in return they get something personal: a painted Home Portrait of their home. Because they get something back, they answer honestly and they finish.

Four reasons it works. One, they get something back. Two, the dream comes first, so nobody bails at a hard question about land or money. Three, buyers sort themselves. Their own answers pick their portrait, so nobody on our side has to guess what kind of buyer they are. And four, it asks your first call questions for you. Who lives there, what they love, their land, their region, how they decide, and when they want keys. Those are eight answers you would normally spend twenty minutes collecting.

Here is the quiz at a glance. This is the first screen a buyer sees after they tap one of the Home Portrait ads. It lives on our own site, mitchellhomesliving.com slash portrait. Scan the code or click the link and try it yourself on your phone after this meeting. It really does take about ninety seconds.

Notice what it promises: answer eight questions about the home and the land, and we paint your Home Portrait. It also tells them up front that every Mitchell home includes five thousand to twenty five thousand dollars in Mitchell Design Dollars.

The most important thing about the quiz is the order. We ask about the home first, the land in the middle, and timing last. You will see why when we walk through the questions.

Here is The Home Portrait from the buyer's side, in five moments.

One, the ad. There are five of them, each written for a different kind of buyer. Two, the quiz. Eight questions, about ninety seconds. Three, the portrait. The buyer gets a painted home and a personal story built from their answers. Four, Design Dollars, which every portrait explains. Five, your desk. Every answer goes into Homebuilder Studio, and the buyer has already seen their portrait.

Every slide in this section is just a closer look at one of these five.

These are the five Home Portrait ads, as the buyer sees them in their feed. Each one has a single photo, a short hook, and one button: Take the Quiz. There is no painting in the ad on purpose. The painting is the reward they get after the quiz.

Each ad also runs in two or three wording variations and in video, so you may hear a buyer quote a slightly different headline. Same buyer, same promise.

There is no Planner ad in this set. Planners click whichever ad speaks to their situation, or the Planner ad in the Four Buyers campaign, and the quiz figures out that they are a Planner from how they answer.

This is the Value Unlocker ad, and this buyer is our priority. They already own land, or there is family land in the picture. On the left is the clean version, on the right is how it looks in a real feed.

What stopped them from building? Somebody told them custom means a big pile of cash and a construction loan. The ad goes straight at that: your land can be your down payment. Zero down, zero closing costs, no construction loan, on approved terms.

When these buyers finish the quiz, most of them get The Landowner's Portrait. When you call them, they are expecting to talk about their land and the math.

The Grounded Dreamer. This buyer can already see the house. They know the porch, the kitchen, the feel. The ad invites them to discover their Home Portrait: their style, their spaces, their plan.

What stopped them? Fear that custom building means a thousand decisions, surprise costs, and a dream that gets away from them.

Their portrait is The Dreamer's Portrait. What they need to hear from you: your vision stays yours, and our process keeps it standing on solid ground. Forty plus plans, forty thousand plus selections, and guardrails at every turn.

The Transitioner. Life is moving for this family. Kids are growing, or a parent is moving in, or two households are becoming one. The ad talks about the home your family grows into, not out of, and room for every generation.

What stopped them? Their life is already full. Building sounded like one more overwhelming project.

They get The Family Portrait. Your job on the phone is to make it feel small and doable. Big decisions become small steps, and we carry the heavy ones.

The Land Seeker. This buyer wants a custom home but has no land yet. The ad says it plainly: no land yet, start here. Dream the home first, then find the land together.

What stopped them? They did not know where to begin, or how to judge what a lot will really cost once you add the county rules, well, and septic.

There is no Land Seeker portrait. These buyers get whichever of the four portraits fits their answers, in the no land version. That version tells them they are closer than they think, and that our team helps them evaluate every lot before they buy. So on the first call, ask where they have been looking.

The Gathering Place. This is the newest ad, for buyers dreaming about the getaway they keep promising themselves. A lake house, a place on the coast, a spot in the mountains, or the place they plan to retire.

What stopped them? Second home financing. Banks ask for bigger down payments and tougher terms when the home is not your main address.

Because Mitchell self funds every build, there is no construction loan. That is the whole message: the second home banks make hard, Mitchell makes simple. These buyers get The Gathering Place Portrait, which we will look at in a few minutes.

The first four questions are all about the home. Who will call it home. Where they are on a Saturday morning. The spaces they cannot live without, up to three. And what the home should say when someone pulls up the driveway.

Why start here? Because it is fun, and because it gets them dreaming before we ask anything hard. By question four they have pictured their porch, their kitchen, their people.

For you, these answers are gold. You will know who lives in the house, their must haves, and their style before you ever say hello. Question three also tells us how much they are likely to personalize, which matters for Design Dollars.

Question five is the land question, and it sits right in the middle on purpose.

If we opened with do you own land, half the people who do not would leave. Asked here, after they have already built the home in their head, it feels like the natural next step. And the screen says it out loud: no land yet is a great answer too.

There are four answers: I own my land, there is family land in the picture, I am looking, or still dreaming. That one answer decides which version of the portrait they get and what the SimplyMitchell section tells them. Landowners hear that their land can be their down payment. Everyone else hears that our team helps them find and evaluate land. When a lead lands on your desk, the land answer is the first thing to look at.

The last three questions. Six is where the home will rise. There are ten choices: our five divisions, four getaway regions like Smith Mountain Lake and the Outer Banks, and somewhere else or still deciding. This is how the lead gets to the right division.

Seven is my favorite for you: how do you make a big decision? Map every step first, run the numbers, picture the end result, or take small steps. That answer tells you exactly how to talk to this person.

Eight is timing, from as soon as possible to someday.

The fourth screen here only appears if they pick one of the lake, coastal, or mountain regions. It asks whether this will be their every day home, a getaway or family retreat, or the place they plan to retire. Everyone else still sees exactly eight questions.

After question eight, the buyer is asked for a first name and email so we can send the full portrait. Then the reveal.

The result screen shows a painting of a home in their region, the name of their portrait, a short story built from their answers, and the SimplyMitchell section for their land situation. It also ties Design Dollars to the first must have they picked. If they chose a chef's kitchen, it tells them that is exactly where Design Dollars work.

One honest note: buyers can skip the email and still see the portrait. So the ones who do give us their name are telling you something.

Now the portraits. The quiz paints one of four core portraits: The Landowner's Portrait for Value Unlockers, The Dreamer's Portrait, The Family Portrait for Transitioners, and The Planner's Portrait.

Each of those comes in two versions, depending on the land answer. If they own land or have family land, the portrait tells them their land can be their down payment. If they have no land yet, it tells them they are closer than they think and that we help them find and evaluate land. Four times two is eight.

The ninth is The Gathering Place, our newest, for second homes and retirement places. The painting changes by region too, so a Raleigh buyer sees a Carolina home and a lake buyer sees a lake home.

Here are the four core portraits side by side. The line in bold italics at the bottom of each card is the actual closing line printed on their portrait, so if you echo it back, they will recognize it.

The Landowner runs the numbers. They need to hear that their land is worth more than they think, and they want the math.

The Dreamer sees the finished home first. They need to hear that the vision stays theirs and the path is clear.

The Family portrait is for a family in a full season. They need to hear that we break big decisions into small steps and carry the heavy ones.

The Planner maps every step. They need to hear that the path is predictable: every step named, every cost on the table, about one hundred fifty days once we break ground.

The Gathering Place is the newest portrait, and it only shows up in one situation. The buyer has to pick one of the four getaway regions: Shenandoah Valley, Smith Mountain Lake, Lake Gaston, or the Eastern Shore and Outer Banks. And they have to tell us it is a getaway, a family retreat, or the place they plan to retire. If they say it will be their every day home, they get one of the other four portraits.

This buyer is picturing the long table, the full house weekends, the dock or the porch or the firepit. The painting changes for lake, coast, or mountains.

What they need to hear: banks make second homes hard. Bigger down payments, tougher terms. Mitchell self funds every build, so there is no construction loan, and if they own the land it works as their equity. The second home banks make hard, Mitchell makes simple.

When a buyer taps See My Full Portrait, or opens the email, they get a thirteen screen presentation built from their answers. These screenshots are from a real run of the live quiz.

It opens with their painted home, then walks through a day in that home, their spaces, an inspiration board, the SimplyMitchell section for their land, their Design Dollars, what their region is like, the roadmap from portrait to keys, and three Behind the Build episodes picked for them.

It ends with one next step: schedule a visit to their Design Studio. So when you call, you are not starting the conversation. You are picking up where their portrait left off.

Every Home Portrait explains Mitchell Design Dollars, so every lead has already heard about it.

Here is how it works. Every Mitchell home starts with five thousand dollars in Design Dollars. The more the buyer personalizes, the more Mitchell adds, up to twenty five thousand. The ladder: twenty five thousand in selections adds seventy five hundred, forty thousand adds eleven thousand, sixty thousand adds fifteen thousand, eighty thousand adds twenty thousand, and one hundred thousand or more adds the full twenty five thousand.

The way to say it is spend and add. Choose sixty thousand in selections, Mitchell adds fifteen thousand, and you take home seventy five thousand worth. Lead with the twenty five thousand, land on the five thousand.

Scott's two sentences are on the slide. Use them word for word. And at the design table, tell the buyer the gap to the next tier.

It covers Design Center items only: cabinets, countertops, flooring, tile, trim, doors, lighting, plumbing fixtures, appliances, paint, and hardware. It does not cover structural options, decks, garages, basements, well, septic, or site work, it never comes off the base price, and it has no cash value.

This is the intel. Now your desk. Every answer from the quiz goes directly into Homebuilder Studio, on the contact record, and the lead is tagged with their persona.

Walk down the table. Question one tells you who lives there, so you know who to invite to the Design Studio and which plans to show. Question two gives you their signature space, which is your easiest opening line. Question three is their must haves, up to three, which drives plan matches and tells you how much they are likely to personalize. Question four is their style.

Question five, the land, is the big one. Owns it, family land, looking, or still dreaming. That tells you whether the first conversation is about their land as a down payment or about helping them find land.

Six is the region, which routes the lead to the right division. Seven is how they decide, which tells you how to sell to this person. Eight is their timeline. And for the getaway regions, you also learn whether this is an every day home, a getaway, or a retirement place.

The point: before you pick up the phone, you already know what most first calls spend twenty minutes finding out.

Here is the same buyer, two ways. On the left, a typical form fill: name, email, phone, interested in building. You start from zero.

On the right, the same buyer as a Home Portrait lead in Homebuilder Studio. This is sample data, but it shows exactly what you get. The yellow tags across the top are the four you will sort and filter by: her persona, her land status, her region, and her timeline. Below that, the rest of her answers: a growing family, happiest outside working on a project, a chef's kitchen, covered outdoor living and a home office, a solid and enduring style, and she decides by running the numbers.

And she has already seen her portrait. Treat this like a warm conversation that is already under way, because it is.

So how do you open that first call with a Home Portrait lead? Three moves.

One, open with their portrait. Say the portrait name and the region. They just saw it, and hearing it back tells them you actually looked.

Two, ask about one thing they picked. A must have space, the land, or the people who will live there. It shows you listened, and it gets them talking about the part they care about.

Three, offer the next step their portrait already named. For most buyers that is a Design Studio visit. For landowners it can be a land walk.

Here is an example: Hi Sarah, this is Dana with Mitchell Homes. Your Home Portrait just came through, the Landowner's Portrait in Central Virginia. I loved that you picked a chef's kitchen and a covered porch. Tell me about your land.

What not to say: so, what are you looking for? They already told us, in eight questions.

Here is a cheat sheet. One opener for each portrait.

The Landowner: lead with the land and the math. Ask how much land they have and whose name it is in.

The Dreamer: lead with the vision. Ask what they see first when they picture pulling up the driveway.

The Family: lead with the people. Ask who will be living in the home.

The Planner: lead with the roadmap. Offer to walk them through every step, from today to their keys.

The Gathering Place: lead with the place. Ask who they picture there with them. Then, when it fits, bring up that there is no construction loan, which is the part banks make hard on a second home.

And for anyone with no land yet, whatever their portrait, ask where they have been looking and offer to help evaluate a lot before they buy.

Every home Mitchell builds is a portrait of its owner. That is the whole idea behind this campaign.

By the time a Home Portrait lead reaches you, your buyer has already seen their portrait. They have pictured the home, answered the land question, and read about SimplyMitchell and Design Dollars. Start the conversation there, and you are already three steps ahead of a form fill.

Before your next shift, take the quiz yourself at mitchellhomesliving.com slash portrait, so you have seen exactly what your buyers see.

Questions?
